rows.verdict: Uniswap v4 arbitrage bot with Balancer flash liquidity
rows.mechanism: hand-written, dispatcherless MEV bot: takes flash liquidity from the Balancer v2 Vault, trades against Uniswap v4 through the PoolManager's lock/settle interface, and pays the builder directly

checks.detail: transient storage (EIP-1153): reentrancy locks, flash accounting
pays or reads the block builder (MEV)
can destroy itself / force-send its balance

rows.unchecked_opinion: settle()/sync(address)/clear(address,uint256)/exttload(bytes32) are the Uniswap v4 PoolManager's own interface, and exttload reads v4's transient storage — so the transient-storage sites are the v4 flash-accounting lock rather than a reentrancy guard. token0()/token1() means it also reads v2/v3-style pairs. Zero logs across 414 calls is the point: an event reader sees the pools move and never sees who moved them. The vanity address (nine zero bytes) is calldata-cost optimisation. UNVERIFIED: that the Balancer leg is a flash loan rather than a plain swap — that needs a trace.

rows.verdict: single-operator MEV bot, one caller, WETH-settled
rows.mechanism: one hardcoded operator drives it 284 times in ten hours; it unwraps WETH and pays the block builder; it emits nothing

checks.detail: pays or reads the block builder (MEV)
transient storage (EIP-1153): reentrancy locks, flash accounting
never writes storage: a router, a lens, or a pure library

rows.unchecked_opinion: The single entry point 0xcabcfc90 has no known signature, which is what a private bot looks like. 0xc0ffeebabe… is a vanity counterparty. UNVERIFIED: what strategy it runs — the bytecode says how it settles, not what it trades.

rows.verdict: address-poisoning executor, delegated into EOAs by EIP-7702
rows.mechanism: one function, executeBatch, callable only when tx.origin equals an operator baked into the code; delegated to thousands of accounts so their dust transfers appear to come from thousands of distinct senders

checks.detail: never writes storage: a router, a lens, or a pure library

rows.unchecked_opinion: CONFIRMED independently after the fact: Etherscan's verified source names the contract Poisoner and the immutable thief. tx.origin rather than msg.sender is what lets the operator drive an account it does not otherwise control, through a hub contract in the middle.

rows.verdict: the operator's batch hub for the poisoning campaign
rows.mechanism: same executeBatch, but the owner lives in storage slot 0 and is checked against msg.sender; it calls each delegated account in turn and reverts the whole batch if any leg fails

checks.detail: compares msg.sender against a stored/hardcoded value
never writes storage: a router, a lens, or a pure library

rows.unchecked_opinion: Mutable owner in storage where the delegate has an immutable one — the hub can change hands, the delegation cannot.

rows.verdict: not a program: an SVG stored as contract code
rows.mechanism: SSTORE2-style data contract — a leading STOP byte so the body can never execute, then 24,000 bytes of markup
rows.unchecked_opinion: The body begins `<svg xmlns=...viewBox="0 0 48 48" shape-rendering="crispEdges">`: 48x48 pixel art with a Gaussian-blur glow filter, fully on chain. One deployer wrote twelve of these in the window. The first sweep of this window ranked three such blobs as its most capable contracts, because a linear sweep over stored bytes yields an opcode per byte.

rows.verdict: signature-gated trading executor delegated into EOAs, failing 99% of the time
rows.mechanism: 17 KB EIP-7702 delegate that routes through WETH and the Uniswap v2 and v3 routers under a signed, expiring authorisation
rows.unchecked_opinion: EXPIRED and BAD_SIG are the two revert reasons of a deadline-plus-signature scheme, which fits a wallet that executes orders its user signed offline. In this window its relayer paid $88 of fees for 5 successful transactions out of 533. UNVERIFIED: whose wallet product this is — no verified source, and the selectors resolve to nothing.
